ann_115.original: Node 663 is a ReLU of capital gain (directly and through the inner ReLU node 3460) with a small private work-class term; its closed form is attached as analytical_formula evidence (in z-scores, not dollars), and the rounded formula is off by up to 0.0019 on the training rows. Hypothesis: this is a capital-gain threshold gate that adds a second, steeper downward push on the predicted chance of a low income (an income of $50,000 or less) for people with large capital gains, on top of capital gain's direct edge (weight -3.38 per sd, in direct_linear). Testable threshold, self-probed: holding the typical case, the gate is closed at 4400 US dollars (node 663 = 0.00) and open at 4600 US dollars (node 663 = 0.016); its inner unit, node 3460, opens a little later (node 3460 = 0.024 at 5000 US dollars) and makes the gate steeper. In the whole model the predicted risk of this typical case falls from 72% at 0 US dollars to below 1% at 15000 US dollars, with node 663 = 2.29 there. In the training data the gate is open for 2143 people (5.5% of rows); for them it changes the score by -2.90 logits on average through this part, and their observed low-income rate is 14.6% against a mean predicted risk of 10.4%. Another 1142 people have a smaller, non-zero capital gain that leaves the gate closed; for them capital gain acts through its direct edge. The private work-class term moves the threshold very little (its coefficient in the attached formula). Switching the gate off changes the training AUC from 0.9074 to 0.9069.

Hypothesis: the chain makes shorter working weeks raise the predicted chance of a low income, with a hinge at about 50 hours (above it the part is flat) and a second, steeper segment for very short weeks. Self-probe, sweeping hours on the typical case (part contributions are measured against the part's baseline, node 4445 at zero and node 5856 at its training mean): node 4445 is 0.207 at 45 hours and 0.00 at 50 hours; from 50 hours to 80 hours the part's contribution stays at -0.066 (it is -0.066 at the top of the sweep), so above the hinge hours act through their direct edge (weight -0.21 per sd) and the whole-model risk drifts from 59% to 46%. Below the hinge the part's contribution rises to 1.21 logits at 20 hours. The last node, 11637, is closed at 18 hours (value 0.00) and open at 15 hours (value 0.010), and adds more for shorter weeks: at 1 hours the part contributes 2.16 logits and the whole-model risk is 97%, against 72% at 40 hours. In the training data node 4445 is positive for 31,364 people; 31,364 people work under 50 hours, and 0 people working that much or more have node 4445 positive. Node 11637 is open for 1674 people, whose observed low-income rate is 92.4% (mean predicted 92.7%). Being born in Thailand closes node 11637: for a Thailand-born typical case working 10 hours its value is 0.00; this exception is fitted to the 26 Thailand-born training people. Switching the part off changes the training AUC from 0.9074 to 0.9044, the largest loss among the hidden parts.
ann_116.proposed: A working-hours part that lowers the predicted chance of a low income in an uneven way as weekly hours rise while they stay below about 50 hours, with no further change above that: for a typical person from about 87% at 17 hours to about 63% at 99 hours.

ann_117.proposed: A preschool step: for a typical person whose highest education is preschool, the predicted chance of a low income rises from about 72% to above 99%; a protective-service occupation barely changes it.

Hypothesis: an either-or gate that opens for people who work without pay or were born in Iran and then raises their predicted chance of a low income; an other-service occupation by itself does not open it. ann_120.original: Four single-input ReLU units, each fed by one category indicator: node 5995 (bachelor's degree), node 11222 (unmarried, relationship code 4), node 13264 (born in Honduras) and node 13622 (professional-school degree). The closed form is attached as analytical_formula evidence (z-scores), and the rounded formula is off by up to 0.012 on the training rows. Because each indicator takes two values, each unit takes two values and acts as an extra score offset for its category, on top of the direct edges. Hypothesis and self-probes, one per unit. Unmarried: through this part being unmarried lowers the score (for the typical case set to divorced and living outside a family, node 11222 goes from 0.44 to 4.13 and its edge into the output has weight -0.451), yet in the whole model this unmarried case gets a higher predicted risk than the same case not in a family (97% against 96%), because not being in a family carries its own direct edge (weight -0.88 per sd) and being unmarried has none; for the 4059 unmarried people the part's mean contribution is -1.49 logits. Honduras: for the typical case, being born in Honduras raises node 13264 to 52.6 (output weight -0.076) and drops the predicted risk from 72% to 5%; this offset is fitted to the 14 Honduras-born training people and goes against them, since their observed low-income rate is 85.7% while their mean predicted risk is 62.4%. Professional school: for the typical case (education level held at its typical value) it lowers the predicted risk from 72% to 68% with node 13622 = 7.70 (output weight -0.024); 652 training people hold this degree. Bachelor's degree: node 5995 goes from 0.11 to 0.00 with output weight 0.028, so this unit barely moves the score; the rise in this probe's risk (from 72% to 76%, education level held fixed) comes through the bachelor's direct edge (weight 0.082 per sd). Switching the four units off changes the training AUC from 0.9074 to 0.9060.
ann_120.proposed: Four single-category adjustments that lower the predicted chance of a low income: being unmarried in the household (to about 33% for a typical person), being born in Honduras (to about 5%, from 14 training people), a professional school degree (to about 68%) and a bachelor's degree (about 72%).

ann_121.original: The direct input-to-output edges, gathered at identity node identity_0: a linear score in the z-scored inputs, attached as analytical_formula evidence (the rounded formula is off by up to 0.046 on the training rows). The largest direct weights (per sd, each through its own edge) lower the predicted chance of a low income: capital gain -3.38, husband -1.26, education level -1.09, wife -0.97, married to a civilian spouse -0.89, not in a family -0.88, age -0.59, male sex -0.52, capital loss -0.31, executive or managerial work -0.28 and weekly hours -0.21; the largest raising weights are other-service work 0.54, born in Colombia 0.32 and never worked 0.31. Self-probe: age is not an input of any hidden part (see the entry lists), so a sweep shows the linear term; for the typical case the score falls from 1.472 at 25 years to 1.046, 0.620, 0.194 and -0.232 at 65 years, and the predicted risk from 81% to 44%. Raising the education level from 9 on the 1-16 scale to 13 on the 1-16 scale (education category held) moves the typical risk from 72% to 32%.

ann_122.original: The output node adds the direct linear score (identity_0) and the weighted exits of the six hidden parts to a bias and applies a sigmoid, so the predicted chance of a low income is sigmoid(score); the formula is attached as analytical_formula evidence. No hidden part feeds another part, so the parts combine by addition on the score (logit) scale. Hypothesis: the model is a linear logit score (direct_linear) with additive corrections for large capital gains, short working weeks, never-married status (12,914 people) and a few small categories (preschool, without pay, Iran, Honduras, unmarried, professional school). Self-probe of additivity: for the typical case living outside a family, being never married rather than married to a civilian spouse moves the score from 1.501 to 3.607 with no capital gain and from -7.432 to -5.326 with a capital gain of 15000 US dollars: an equal step on the score, while on the risk scale the change is from 82% to 97% in the first case and from 0.06% to 0.48% in the second. On the 39,073 training rows the mean predicted risk is 75.0% against an observed low-income rate of 76.1%. The training AUC is 0.9074; with all six hidden parts switched off, leaving the linear score, it is 0.9021, so the hidden parts add a little ranking power on top of a mostly linear model. The replayed model matches the original network to within 6.7e-16.
ann_122.proposed: The model adds up seven parts on one score: a weighted sum of every input plus adjustments for large capital gains, short working weeks, preschool education, never-married status, working without pay or being born in Iran, and four single categories; for a typical person it predicts about 72% chance of a low income, and higher capital gains lower that slowly at first, then faster, to about 7% at 6849 US dollars.

Hypothesis: the model is a linear logit score (direct_linear) with additive corrections for large capital gains, short working weeks, never-married status (12,914 people) and a few small categories (preschool, without pay, Iran, Honduras, unmarried, professional school). parts.name: hours_chain
parts.original_hypothesis: Nodes 4445, 5856, 10780 and 11637 form a serial chain of ReLUs on weekly working hours, with a Thailand-of-birth term at the last node; the closed form is attached as analytical_formula evidence (in z-scores, not hours), and the rounded formula is off by up to 0.0021 on the training rows. Hypothesis: the chain makes shorter working weeks raise the predicted chance of a low income, with a hinge at about 50 hours (above it the part is flat) and a second, steeper segment for very short weeks. Self-probe, sweeping hours on the typical case (part contributions are measured against the part's baseline, node 4445 at zero and node 5856 at its training mean): node 4445 is 0.207 at 45 hours and 0.00 at 50 hours; from 50 hours to 80 hours the part's contribution stays at -0.066 (it is -0.066 at the top of the sweep), so above the hinge hours act through their direct edge (weight -0.21 per sd) and the whole-model risk drifts from 59% to 46%. Below the hinge the part's contribution rises to 1.21 logits at 20 hours. The last node, 11637, is closed at 18 hours (value 0.00) and open at 15 hours (value 0.010), and adds more for shorter weeks: at 1 hours the part contributes 2.16 logits and the whole-model risk is 97%, against 72% at 40 hours. In the training data node 4445 is positive for 31,364 people; 31,364 people work under 50 hours, and 0 people working that much or more have node 4445 positive. Node 11637 is open for 1674 people, whose observed low-income rate is 92.4% (mean predicted 92.7%). Being born in Thailand closes node 11637: for a Thailand-born typical case working 10 hours its value is 0.00; this exception is fitted to the 26 Thailand-born training people. Switching the part off changes the training AUC from 0.9074 to 0.9044, the largest loss among the hidden parts.

parts.name: without_pay_or_iran_gate
parts.original_hypothesis: Node 443 is a ReLU of the without-pay work-class, other-service occupation and Iran-of-birth indicators; the closed form is attached as analytical_formula evidence (z-scores), and the rounded formula is off by up to 0.016 on the training rows. Hypothesis: an either-or gate that opens for people who work without pay or were born in Iran and then raises their predicted chance of a low income; an other-service occupation by itself does not open it. In the training data it is open for 67 people; 17 people work without pay and 50 were born in Iran, 0 open rows lie outside these two groups and 0 rows inside them have it closed. reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient); an input the data ties to a category takes its typical value within that category (linked inputs)

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients

confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points

For a typical person, the model gives a lower predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) if the highest education is professional school degree (with education level (1 = preschool to 16 = doctorate) at 15 on the 1-16 scale, as in the data) (about 14%) than if highest education is something other than 10th grade, preschool, professional school degree, some college, 5th-6th grade, 7th-8th grade, associate degree (academic), associate degree (vocational), bachelor's degree (about 72%) (on the training data only).

The model treats a higher education level as clearly lowering the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) in an uneven way: for a typical person, it goes from about 86% at 7 on the 1-16 scale to about 37% at 13 on the 1-16 scale (with highest education at bachelor's degree, as in the data).

Through one part of the model, weekly working hours only clearly lowers the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) while it stays below about 50 hours: for a typical such person, going from 17 hours to 99 hours moves it from about 87% to about 63%; across patients the change happens in an uneven way.
